title: Getting Emails Meant for Someone Else? Why It Happens and What to Do
html:
Getting mail meant for someone else almost always has a plain reason: Gmail ignores dots in addresses, someone typed your address when signing up, or a person set up forwarding to your address by mistake. Check each cause below before you assume your account has been hacked.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. This page covers Gmail; other providers have their own help pages.

Sources last checked: 10 Oct 2026.

Reasons you get someone else's email

  • Dots in the address. Gmail ignores periods. If your address is johnsmith@gmail.com, you also receive mail sent to john.smith@gmail.com. Google's words: you own all the dotted versions of your address. Someone with a similar name may be giving out the wrong version.
  • An accidental or false sign-up. Someone used your address for a newsletter, a shop or a promotion.
  • Forwarding. Someone may have set up automatic forwarding from their Gmail to yours.
  • Bcc. If you were added by Bcc, your address may not appear at the top of the message.
  • Gmail and Googlemail. In some regions, @gmail.com and @googlemail.com reach the same inbox.

How to check for forwarding

Open a message that looks like it was sent to you by mistake. Tap or click More next to Reply, then Show original, and look for "X-Forwarded-For". If you see it, someone is forwarding their messages to your address. Google suggests contacting that person to let them know about the mistake.

How to stop it

  1. For newsletters and promotions: open the email, tap Unsubscribe next to the sender's name, then tap Unsubscribe or Go to website in the pop-up. It may take a few days to stop.
  2. For anything else: report it as spam, or block the sender. Blocking does not unsubscribe you; future mail from that sender just goes to Spam.
  3. Do not reply to the sender, and do not click links in a message that is not for you. If it asks you to confirm something, ignore it.

See what to do if emails continue after unsubscribing.

When it might mean someone is in your account

Mail meant for someone else is not a sign of a hack by itself. These are:

  • sent messages you did not write,
  • security alerts about a new sign-in or a changed password,
  • a forwarding rule or filter you did not create in Gmail settings,
  • a device in your account you do not recognise.

If you see any of these, follow Google's steps for securing a compromised account: review your devices and security events, change your password, and turn on 2-Step Verification. Our Google account checklist goes through it.

What to do next

  1. Look at one misdirected message with Show original.
  2. Unsubscribe or report spam.
  3. Check Gmail settings for forwarding or filters you did not create.
